We proceed by setting the lower bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to -\infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{-3}7{e}^{x}\,\text{d}x & =7\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{-3}{e}^{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =7\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }{[{e}^{x}]}_{a}^{-3} \\  & =7\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }({e}^{-3}-{e}^{a}) \\  & =7\cdot (\frac{1}{{e}^{3}}-{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{e}^{a})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall the end behavior of the function $y={e}^{x}$ shown in the graph below:

- ${lim}_{x\to -\infty }{e}^{x}=0$

- ${lim}_{x\to \infty }{e}^{x}=\infty $

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14042659/assets/4af4a2b7389d3773cc71e843190c6ab111355248a15e6165a8e39e37252061b9.png)

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{-3}7{e}^{x}\,\text{d}x & =7\cdot (\frac{1}{{e}^{3}}-{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{e}^{a}) \\  & =7(\frac{1}{{e}^{3}}-0) \\  & =\frac{7}{{e}^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
First, we substitute $u=2+{x}^{3}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=3{x}^{2}\,⟹\,\frac{1}{3}\text{d}u={x}^{2}\text{d}x.
$$

Since $u\to -\infty $ when $x\to -\infty ,$ the table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=2+{x}^{3}$ is as follows:

| $x$ | $1$ | $-\infty $ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $3$ | $-\infty $ |

So, the integral in terms of the new variable $u$ is

$$
{\int }_{-\infty }^{1}{x}^{2}{e}^{2+{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{-\infty }^{3}{e}^{u}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Now, we proceed by setting the lower bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to -\infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{1}{x}^{2}{e}^{2+{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{3}{e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }[{e}^{u}]_{a}^{3} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }({e}^{3}-{e}^{a}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot ({e}^{3}-{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{e}^{a})\end{aligned}
$$

Next, recall the end behavior of the function $y={e}^{x},$ shown in the graph below:

- ${lim}_{a\to -\infty }{e}^{x}=0$

- ${lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{x}=\infty $

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14042659/assets/3df1853e93a5ab2a1c1ca4114d450b29a69223bd576b059d9aef1b17c68fe5b7.png)

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{1}{x}^{2}{e}^{2+{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot ({e}^{3}-{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{e}^{a}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot ({e}^{3}-0) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{3}}{3}.\end{aligned}

So, the integral in terms of the new variable $u$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }x{e}^{-{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-u}\,\text{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }x{e}^{-{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{-u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{[-{e}^{-u}]}_{0}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{[{e}^{-u}]}_{0}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\cdot ({lim}_{a\to \infty }\frac{1}{{e}^{a}}-1)\end{aligned}

Now, we proceed by setting the lower bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to -\infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{{e}^{5/x}}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{0}{e}^{5u}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{[\frac{{e}^{5u}}{5}]}_{a}^{0} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}{lim}_{a\to -\infty }(1-{e}^{5a}) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(1-{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{e}^{5a})\end{aligned}
$$

Next, recall the end behavior of the function $y={e}^{5x}$ shown in the graph below:

- ${lim}_{x\to -\infty }{e}^{5x}=0$

- ${lim}_{x\to \infty }{e}^{5x}=\infty $

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14042659/assets/2a24352ca6421b3aa61f3f29e3c19373cca011feafce263775a2f692f67ad36b.png)

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{{e}^{5/x}}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{5}(1-{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{e}^{5a}) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(1-0) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating an Improper Integral Using a Substitution
questions.worked_solution:
First, we substitute $u=\sqrt{1-x}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{1-x}}\,⟹\,-\text{d}u=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{1-x}}\text{d}x.
$$

Since $u\to \infty $ when $x\to -\infty ,$ the table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=\sqrt{1-x}$ is as follows:

| $x$ | $0$ | $-\infty $ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1$ | $\infty $ |

So, the integral in terms of the new variable $u$ is

$$
{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{{e}^{-\sqrt{1-x}}}{2\sqrt{1-x}}\,\text{d}x=-{\int }_{\infty }^{1}{e}^{-u}\,\text{d}u={\int }_{1}^{\infty }{e}^{-u}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Now, we proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to \infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{{e}^{-\sqrt{1-x}}}{2\sqrt{1-x}}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{1}^{a}{e}^{-u}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }[-{e}^{-u}]_{1}^{a} \\  & =\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }(-\frac{1}{{e}^{a}}+\frac{1}{e}) \\  & =\frac{1}{e}-{lim}_{a\to \infty }\frac{1}{{e}^{a}}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, recall the end behavior of the function $y=\frac{1}{{e}^{x}}$ shown in the graph below:

- ${lim}_{a\to -\infty }\frac{1}{{e}^{x}}=\infty $

- ${lim}_{a\to \infty }\frac{1}{{e}^{x}}=0$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14042659/assets/4ef3194e946aec805866202a5e0ad521291d71b1fabc2df68d6cb1a4d93da42b.png)

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{{e}^{-\sqrt{1-x}}}{2\sqrt{1-x}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{e}-{lim}_{a\to \infty }\frac{1}{{e}^{a}} \\  & =\frac{1}{e}-0 \\  & =\frac{1}{e}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Improper Integral Involving the Exponential Function
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the following result:

$$
\int e^{px + q}\,\textrm d x = \dfrac1p e^{px+q} + C
$$

We proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to\infty.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{\infty }{e}^{-3x}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{-1}^{a}{e}^{-3x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{[-\frac{{e}^{-3x}}{3}\,]}_{-1}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{[{e}^{-3x}]}_{-1}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\cdot ({lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-3a}-{e}^{3})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall the end behavior of the function $y=e^{-3x}$ shown in the graph below:

- $\lim\limits_{x \to -\infty} e^{-3x} = \infty$

- $\lim\limits_{x \to \infty} e^{-3x} =0$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14042659/assets/bc4ffc41105491f2bd6b37b2482afc64946d8f67f6db83dfa322c400ae4bc2b6.png)

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{\infty }{e}^{-3x} & =-\frac{1}{3}\cdot ({lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-3a}-{e}^{3}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\cdot (0-{e}^{3}) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{3}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Improper Integral Involving Other Exponential Functions
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the following result:

$$
\int b^{\,px + q}\,\textrm d x = \dfrac1{p\ln(b)} b^{\,px+q} + C
$$

We proceed by setting the lower bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to-\infty.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}3\cdot {2}^{2x+1}\,\text{d}x & =3\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{0}{2}^{2x+1}\,\text{d}x \\  & =3\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }{[\frac{{2}^{2x+1}}{2\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}]}_{a}^{0} \\  & =\frac{3\cdot {2}^{1}}{2\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }{[{2}^{2x}]}_{a}^{0} \\  & =\frac{3}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }({2}^{0}-{2}^{2a}) \\  & =\frac{3}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}\cdot (1-{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{2}^{2a})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall the end behavior of the function $y=2^{2x}$ shown in the graph below:

- $\lim\limits_{x \to -\infty} 2^{2x} = 0$

- $\lim\limits_{x \to \infty} 2^{2x} = \infty$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14042659/assets/009f467677932d0ac17e1632c31f4d3aa5271ffe332730d9670e69862b243bef.png)

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}3\cdot {2}^{2x+1}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{3}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}\cdot (1-{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{2}^{2a}) \\  & =\frac{3}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}\cdot (1-0) \\  & =\frac{3}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating an Improper Integral Using a Substitution
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we substitute $u=x^4.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}= 4x^3
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\dfrac 14 \textrm{d}u =x^3\textrm{d}x.
$$

Since $u\to \infty$ when $x\to \infty,$ the table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=x^4$ is as follows:

| $x$ | $1$ | $\infty$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1$ | $\infty$ |

So, the integral in terms of the new variable $u$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{\infty }{x}^{3}\cdot {2}^{-{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{1}^{\infty }{2}^{-u}\,\text{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to\infty.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{\infty }{x}^{3}\cdot {2}^{-{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{1}^{\infty }{2}^{-u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{1}^{a}{2}^{-u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{[-\frac{{2}^{-u}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}]}_{1}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{1}{4\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{[{2}^{-u}]}_{1}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{1}{4\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\cdot ({lim}_{a\to \infty }\frac{1}{{2}^{a}}-\frac{1}{2})\end{aligned}
$$

Next, recall the end behavior of the function $y=\dfrac{1}{2^x},$ shown in the graph below:

- $\lim\limits_{x \to -\infty} \dfrac{1}{2^{x}} = \infty$

- $\lim\limits_{x \to \infty} \dfrac{1}{2^{x}} = 0$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14042659/assets/1969145d74662468ec23d458ac1ad0194d51cbf6b026718b7232466e9357efdf.png)

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{\infty }{x}^{3}\cdot {2}^{-{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x & =-\frac{1}{4\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\cdot ({lim}_{a\to \infty }\frac{1}{{2}^{a}}-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{4\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\cdot (0-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{8\operatorname{ln}⁡2}.\end{aligned}
$$
